summary: This document defines usage profiles for DNS over TLS and DTLS, built on one or more authentication mechanisms. They can improve the privacy of DNS lookups compared to plain text. It also specifies new authentication mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS questions are normally sent like postcards. This describes ways to put them in a private envelope and make sure you are talking to the right server.

subtitle: Two usage profiles, Strict and Opportunistic, and the ways a DNS client can check it is really talking to its encrypted DNS server.

tldr.problem: Cleartext DNS can be watched by passive eavesdroppers and tampered with by active attackers who redirect clients to rogue servers, and encryption alone does not say whether the server is the right one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Strict Privacy profile (encryption and authentication required) and an Opportunistic Privacy profile (best effort), the ways to authenticate a server using SPKI pin sets or an authentication domain name, and a (D)TLS protocol profile for DNS.
tldr.outcome: Clients can choose between best protection and best chance of getting an answer, and servers know which credentials and TLS features to offer. The RFC updates RFC 7858.

today: RFC 8310 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It updates RFC 7858 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
DNS privacy issues are discussed in RFC 7626. Two of them matter most here: passive attacks that eavesdrop on cleartext DNS, and active attacks that redirect clients to rogue servers to monitor DNS traffic. RFC 7858 (DNS over TLS) and RFC 8094 (DNS over DTLS, an Experimental specification) give ways to improve privacy between clients and servers. RFC 8310 adds the layer on top: usage profiles and authentication.

The scope is limited to stub clients talking to recursive resolvers. Out of scope are authentication of authoritative servers by recursive resolvers, authentication of clients by servers, the details of SPKI pin set checking (defined in RFC 7858), and any server identifier other than domain names.

A privacy-enabling DNS server MUST implement DNS over TLS, MAY implement DNS over DTLS, SHOULD offer at least one of the credentials described in the RFC, and implements the (D)TLS profile of Section 9.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the phone book a question out loud lets anyone nearby listen in. This RFC is about whispering instead and making sure you whisper to the right person.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A DNS client is a stub resolver or forwarder, and a DNS server is a recursive resolver or forwarder; authoritative servers are not covered. (D)TLS is shorthand for both TLS and DTLS.

An authentication domain name (ADN) is a domain name that can be used to authenticate a privacy-enabling DNS server. An SPKI pin set is a collection of cryptographic digests that pin public key information, similar to HTTP Public Key Pinning, and it constrains a DNS server. A credential is information that proves a server's identity, such as a PKIX certificate or a DNSSEC-validated chain to a TLSA record.
sections.plainLanguage: The server needs a name tag to prove who it is. The name it claims is the authentication domain name, and the proof is its credential.

sections.title: The Two Usage Profiles
sections.content:
The Strict Privacy profile requires both an encrypted and an authenticated connection to a privacy-enabling DNS server. If that is not available, a hard failure occurs. It mitigates both passive and active attacks, but the client may get no DNS service. A client requiring Strict Privacy MUST NOT start sending DNS queries until at least one privacy-enabling DNS server becomes available.

The Opportunistic Privacy profile follows Opportunistic Security (RFC 7435): cleartext is the baseline, with encryption and authentication used when available. The result may be an authenticated and encrypted connection, an encrypted one, or cleartext. It keeps DNS working at the cost of possibly no attack mitigation, and it supports incremental deployment with a view to widespread adoption of Strict Privacy.

A client SHOULD select a profile when resolving a query and MUST NOT fall back from Strict Privacy to Opportunistic Privacy during the resolution of a given query. The Strict profile SHOULD always be implemented in clients that implement the Opportunistic one, and a client SHOULD NOT be configured by default to use only cleartext.

Both profiles may begin with a meta-query, performed with Opportunistic Privacy, to learn the server's IP address. An active attack on that query is possible, and DNSSEC validation can detect it.
sections.plainLanguage: Strict is like refusing to talk unless the door is locked and you know who is inside. Opportunistic is like using the lock if there is one, but still talking if there is not.

sections.title: Authentication Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC lists six ways for a client to get and check authentication information: SPKI pin sets plus an IP address configured out of band; an ADN plus IP address configured out of band; an ADN only, with the IP address learned by meta-queries for A/AAAA records; DHCP, which needs a non-standard or future option to carry the ADN; DANE with a DNSSEC chain obtained by meta-queries; and the TLS DNSSEC chain extension, where the server supplies the chain in the handshake.

Each has trade-offs. For example, DANE needs a DNSSEC-validating stub implementation and leaks meta-queries to a network-provided server, while the TLS extension reduces latency compared with DANE. Under any approach the ADN is leaked in the Server Name Indication field of the ClientHello.

If a client is configured with both an ADN and an SPKI pin set for a server, it SHOULD match on both a valid credential and a valid pin set, and the overall result SHOULD be successful only if both succeed.

With Strict Privacy, a client MUST use either a source of ADNs or an SPKI pin set, MUST only try servers for which it holds at least one piece of authentication information, and MUST abort connections when no verification mechanism succeeds. With Opportunistic Privacy, clients that know authentication information SHOULD still try it, because failure is a sign of a possible active attack.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to learn what a trusted server looks like, such as being told ahead of time or looking it up. If you know two ways, check both.

sections.title: Getting the Authentication Domain Name
sections.content:
A client usually knows only the IP address of its DNS server, so it needs a name to check against. The RFC describes three sources. Full direct configuration gives both the ADN and the IP address through a file or API. Direct configuration of the ADN only lets the client learn the address by asking an untrusted resolver for A/AAAA records; a DNSSEC-validating client SHOULD apply the same validation policy to these meta-queries as to other queries.

Dynamic discovery is not possible by any standard means at the time of writing. A DHCP server normally supplies resolver addresses but no ADN, and this RFC does not request any DHCP extension. If one is developed, the discovery technique MUST be secure and trustworthy when a Strict Privacy profile is used.
sections.plainLanguage: To check someone's name tag you must first know what name to look for. You can be told it directly, or find the address from a helper you do not fully trust.

sections.title: Verifying Credentials
sections.content:
Two domain-name-based checks are defined. For PKIX certificates, a client MUST verify the entire certification path per RFC 5280 and compare the ADN to the certificate using RFC 6125 rules. The reference identifier is a DNS-ID, which is simply the ADN. A compliant client MUST only inspect the subjectAltName extension and MUST NOT inspect the Subject field.

For DANE, the record for a DNS privacy server takes the form _853._tcp.[authentication-domain-name] for TLS and _853._udp.[authentication-domain-name] for DTLS. A client MAY fetch the records itself, using the Opportunistic profile or in the clear, and they MUST be validated with DNSSEC. Alternatively the client MAY offer the TLS DNSSEC chain extension; if it does, it MUST be able to validate the full chain, and if the chain does not validate it MUST ignore it and rely on other credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you know the name, you check the server's ID card. Either an official stamp-checker vouches for it, or a signed entry in the DNS phone book does.

sections.title: The (D)TLS Protocol Profile
sections.content:
Clients and servers MUST follow the recommendations and security considerations of RFC 7525, except for the version. Because encrypting DNS is a greenfield deployment, they MUST implement only (D)TLS 1.2 or later. Implementations MUST NOT offer or provide TLS compression, citing CRIME-style information leaks.

Implementations MUST support TLS session resumption without server-side state (RFC 5077, which this RFC says updates RFC 7858) and raw public keys (RFC 7250). A client MUST only indicate raw public key support if it has an SPKI pin set pre-configured. They SHOULD support TLS False Start (RFC 7918) and the Cached Information Extension (RFC 7924).

Against traffic analysis, clients and servers SHOULD implement EDNS(0) padding (RFC 7830), and clients SHOULD implement the privacy election of RFC 7871 so a resolver does not leak client address information to authoritative servers.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the rules for how the sealed envelope is made: use a modern kind, do not squash it in ways that give clues, and pad it so every envelope looks about the same size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7525, RFC 8094 and RFC 7858 apply. In addition, DNS clients SHOULD support the DANE mechanisms and offer a configuration option that limits authentication to only those mechanisms, with no fallback to pure PKIX, so that relying solely on the PKIX infrastructure can be avoided.

The RFC also notes that an Opportunistic client cannot know why authentication failed, but it should assume an active attack is in progress. In its comparison, an encrypted but unauthenticated connection offers no protection against an active attacker, though detection is possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If the name tag check fails, act as if a trickster might be nearby. You may also choose to trust only the signed phone book entries and not the usual stamp offices.

viz.caption: THE SIX AUTHENTICATION MECHANISMS (SHORT NAMES FROM THE RFC)

items.title: SPKI
items.text: SPKI pin set(s) and IP address obtained out of band.

items.title: ADN
items.text: Authentication domain name and IP address obtained out of band.

items.title: ADN only
items.text: Name configured; IP learned by A/AAAA meta-queries.

items.title: DHCP
items.text: Name and IP from DHCP; needs a non-standard or future option.

items.title: DANE
items.text: DNSSEC chain with TLSA record fetched by meta-queries.

items.title: TLS extension
items.text: DNSSEC chain supplied by the server in the TLS handshake.
